POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Sat, 03 Oct 2026 16:04:54 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.9 Two Iranians charged with alleged bomb plot against Britain’s Jewish community https://www.politico.eu/article/two-iranians-charged-with-alleged-bomb-plot-against-britains-jewish-community/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 03 Oct 2026 16:01:51 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9102125 Two Iranian men have been charged with terror offenses over an alleged plot to bomb Manchester’s Jewish community.

Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, appeared in a British court on Saturday on charges of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism.

Police said the two men, who were arrested last month on the eve of the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, had received material and instructions on how to make a bomb, identified targets and carried out reconnaissance ahead of an attack on Jewish targets.

They also said another man, likely in Iran, was in contact with them over the plot. The arrests followed a joint investigation by counter-terrorism police and the MI5 secret services.

The latest charges follow Prime Minister Andy Burnham announcing there were “strong indications” that Iran was involved in a suspicious incident linked to the RAF Fairford last week, which involved three vans parked strangely and a group of hooded, masked men near the airbase.

Britain’s deputy assistant commissioner for counter-terrorism Vicki Evans said the last week has “brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran,” while adding the two incidents “are not connected in any way.”

British Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said both men had arrived to Britain via small boats in 2020 and 2023. One had been granted asylum and the other had an asylum application pending.

]]> en Spaniards protest housing crisis as Sánchez weighs snap vote https://www.politico.eu/article/spaniards-protest-housing-crisis-as-pedro-sanchez-weighs-snap-vote/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 03 Oct 2026 15:17:04 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9101948 A wave of housing protests swept across dozens of Spanish cities on Saturday as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez weighed calling a snap election.

The largest demonstration took place in Madrid, where four columns of protesters filled the capital’s main boulevards before converging on Cibeles Square. The Spanish Tenants Union, which organized the protests, said 500,000 people took to the streets, while the government’s delegation in Madrid estimated 70,000 protesters participated.

Spanish Tenants Union spokesperson Valeria Racu said the turnout reflected public exasperation with political leaders who have failed to tackle a housing crisis in which average rents have risen nearly 90% over the past decade.

“The people on the streets once again hold the power,” she said while addressing the demonstration, insisting that their movement would “no longer tolerate inaction.”

The protests were triggered after an investment firm evicted 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment where she had lived since 1956. Sánchez’s government sought to contain the discontent on Tuesday by unveiling two long-delayed bills aimed at curbing speculative practices, extending eviction protections for vulnerable tenants and automatically renewing existing contracts. But conservative lawmakers in parliament rejected both bills on Friday.

Amid the defeat, senior government figures indicated Sánchez — already under pressure over the ongoing migrant crisis in Ceuta and corruption cases involving members of his family and close political allies — was considering calling a snap election in a bid to capitalize on anger over housing.

Saturday’s protests underscored the risks of that strategy. While demonstrators slammed the conservative opposition for voting down the bills, they also accused Sánchez of failing to tackle the housing crisis since taking office in 2018.

“Eight days of people power have achieved more than eight years of progressive government,” Racu said, adding that protesters would continue pressuring politicians “regardless of who governs this country.”

Calling for a general strike to force the adoption of urgent housing measures, Racu said “the feelings of disaffection, desperation, disillusionment and sadness have been replaced by a new energy on the streets.”

As the demonstrations took place, Sánchez remained out of sight, weighing his options. Emiliano García-Page, the Socialist president of Castilla-La Mancha, and the party’s leaders in Extremadura, the Basque Country and Castilla y León on Saturday urged Sánchez to call an early election, saying voters needed to be heard.

Meanwhile, the prospect of an imminent election is prompting Spain’s fractured left to scramble to regroup. With Deputy Prime Minister Yolanda Díaz declining to run for reelection, Health Minister Mónica García and Culture Minister Ernest Urtasun are seen as frontrunners to succeed her in the leadership of the Sumar party.

But Podemos leader Irene Montero is also positioning herself to lead a broader left-wing alliance. So, too, is longtime housing activist and former Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau, who has signaled a willingness to return to frontline politics at the head of a progressive coalition.

The center-right People’s Party leads in electoral polls with 34% support and is open to forming a government with the far-right Vox party, which is polling at 18%. Sánchez’s Socialists are backed by 26% of voters, and would need the fragmented left to unite behind a viable electoral alliance capable of winning enough seats in parliament to form a fresh coalition.

Spain’s housing protests have begun to spill beyond the country’s borders, with similar demonstrations held in Lisbon, Dublin, Potsdam and The Hague. The mobilizations reflect a bloc-wide crisis marked by the lack of affordable homes and governments under pressure to increase housing supply.

The Russian foreign affairs ministry issued a statement on Saturday warning “foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel against remaining in” Kyiv.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered his troops to abandon the rules of war, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the FT this week.

Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi this week said the country faces a $27 billion defense funding gap this year, with Kyiv hoping to cover about $7 billion domestically and looking to partners for the rest.

]]> de Latvian PM faces bittersweet victory in election backdropped by Russia https://www.politico.eu/article/latvia-prime-minister-andris-kulbergs-faces-bittersweet-victory-election-2026/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 03 Oct 2026 02:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9089159 RIGA — Latvia’s populist Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs will face his first electoral test Saturday — but his head start in the polls is unlikely to shield him from coalition headaches in a contest where Ukraine and Russia are looming large.

After a campaign partially fought in Brussels’ corridors, Kulbergs could see two of his allied parties fail to reach the 5% threshold to get seats. And if his centrist allies fail to make it into parliament, the pro-Ukraine prime minister might struggle to get enough backing.

In this worst-case scenario, he may even need to open talks with Ainārs Šlesers, a right-wing veteran of Latvian politics who opposed restrictive tariffs on Russia.

But Kulbergs, who took office in May after his predecessor, Evika Siliņa, was engulfed in backlash over stray Ukrainian drone strikes, dismissed this idea as speculation, as he is aiming to keep Latvia among the EU’s Russia hawks.

Latvian politics spilled into Brussels last week, when a push from France, Luxembourg and Slovakia to delist two Russian billionaires from the EU sanctions list turned into a standoff between Paris and Riga.

Latvia was the last holdout in a decision requiring agreement from all 27 member countries. Kulbergs filmed social media vlogs ranting about the proposed delistings, which would free up the European holdings of the men in question and allow them to travel to the bloc.

In the end, he lost lost that battle, if only partially.

Despite the tycoons being delisted, the overall sanctions regime with almost 3,000 listings is now locked in for three years — a massive achievement considering EU capitals hitherto had to agree every six months. Latvia also said it would start negotiating with France on enhancing military cooperation and initiate talks on Paris’ nuclear deterrence initiative.

Kulbergs’ expected win on Saturday might be just as bittersweet, despite his right-wing United List party polling in first place at around 20% — a good showing in Latvian parliamentary politics.

His center-right partners, New Unity, are struggling to cross the 5% electoral threshold, which would be a floundering performance for a party that has been home to many Latvian prime ministers, including current European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis.

But for the party’s prime ministerial candidate and ex-Finance Minister Arvils Ašeradens, the low polling numbers are simply the “political pendulum which shifts from one way to the other,” he told POLITICO in Riga last month.

During the last election in 2022, New Unity was the major beneficiary of a rally-round-the-flag moment as Russia had just launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But in 2026, voters seem frustrated with Latvia’s high inflation, the ongoing uncertainty surrounding national airline airBaltic and instrumentalized migration orchestrated by Russia and Belarus.

Kulbergs’ other coalition partner, the agrarian Union of Greens and Farmers (known as ZZS), is also polling below the threshold. And if neither party manages to scrape by, it might force Kulbergs to work with the controversial businessman Šlesers, who carefully advocated expanding trade with Russia.

Kulbergs has dismissed this possibility — “as it is given now: no,” he told POLITICO in early September — because he does not trust the people Šlesers has surrounded himself with. Just weeks earlier, however, he had been less definitive, telling POLITICO in July: “I have to see what chess pieces I will get … to make a coalition.”

Šlesers has been a central figure in Latvian politics for decades, most notably as a local “oligarch” who, via family holdings, exerts influence over the Port of Riga. The capital’s harbor has seen its largely Russian and Belarusian hinterland slowly carved off by EU sanctions.  And after Kulbergs slapped 300% tariffs on transited Russian grain this month , Šlesers told Latvian national TV such transit should be allowed, though he supports Ukraine’s EU accession.

Šlesers had distanced himself from politics for a time, after he was caught on tape plotting to divvy up influential posts with fellow oligarchs about 15 years ago. But he has now captured part of the Russian-speaking vote with his conservative-populist rhethoric.

For Latvian political scientist Una Bergmane at the University of Helsinki, there is a clear scenario where Šlesers, a former transport minister, ends up in government. “There is a possibility: If ZZS makes it into the parliament then there might be a temptation [for Kulbergs] to do something with ZZS and Šlesers.”

But it’s not all doom and gloom for the prime minister. Last week’s sanctions standoff could prop him and his New Unity partners up, said Bergmane. “[Foreign Minister Baiba] Braže is the most positively recognizable New Unity member, so everything she does helps the party, but at this point Kulbergs gets most visibility anyway,” she explained. 

Kulbergs’ short time in office could play in his favor too. The prime minister and his party, Bergmane said, are in “this very, very comfortable place where they haven’t been in power for a long time” but still hold the most influential office in the country of 1.9 million.

]]> en ‘Maxi merde’: French presidential campaign rattled by a week of chaos https://www.politico.eu/article/maxi-merde-french-presidential-campaign-rattled-by-a-week-of-chaos/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:59:21 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9100373 PARIS — French schools are getting torched. The far right’s brightest star is fighting for his political life after being accused of antisemitic remarks. And economic indicators are flashing bright red to warn of a potential sovereign debt disaster in the country.

The crises that have rocked France in recent days are exacerbating partisan cleavages in the country’s increasingly no-holds-barred presidential campaign.

In the words of one government adviser: “It’s the maxi merde.”

Though that individual, who was granted anonymity to candidly discuss the current situation, was only referring to the increasingly violent demonstrations outside secondary schools and the government’s slow-footed response to them, it’s a sentiment likely shared by French voters after a week of particularly bleak headlines.

If there are political winners, it’s not immediately clear who they are. Establishment candidates and moderate voices are still struggling to seize the narrative from far-right presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen and her surging far-left challenger Jean-Luc Mélenchon — both of whom want to fundamentally reshape France and its relationship with Europe.

A survey by pollster Odoxa this week found that the French disapprove of the government’s handling of the student school protests, but they also disapprove of Mélenchon and his far-left party France Unbowed’s involvement.

Mélenchon’s allies have joined demonstrators outside schools, saying they were there to show support and protect minors from confrontations with police. But the government and France Unbowed’s political opponents accuse them of fanning the flames of violence — allegations they deny.

“There’s a battle over the narrative” between the political extremes, a Socialist Party adviser said.

Whatever the case, the week’s crises are showing just how nasty the campaign can get with two populist candidates unafraid to stoke partisan divisions leading the polls.

Diversion tactics

The French government has tried to get a grip on the unravelling protests, holding a crisis meeting Thursday and meeting youth representatives on Friday.

“Lecornu is always running behind the crises, he’s always reacting,” said a centrist adviser.

Le Pen, however, blamed agitators for stirring up violence at the protests and accused France Unbowed of “giving a helping hand” to “agents of chaos and insurrection.”

For her National Rally party, the crisis is a useful opportunity to try to convince voters that her party is the best choice for those concerned with public safety.

“We have a government that is incapable of maintaining public order and a left that is stoking the fire,” said National Rally MP Laurent Jacobelli in an interview with POLITICO.

“We are the only legitimate ones when it comes to [security],” he added.

But the unrest is also a useful distraction for Le Pen as her party president and heir apparent, Jordan Bardella, tries to bat down allegations published Monday by investigative outlet Mediapart that he sent antisemitic messages on Facebook Messenger when he was a 17-year-old activist.

Bardella vehemently denied the allegations and vowed to sue Mediapart, but the website on Thursday published another story outlining how it verified the claims, which included screenshots and conversation data downloaded directly from Meta with the help of their sources.

Bardella was tipped to become Le Pen’s prime minister if she came to power, but his future appears to hang on a thread.

“Do we need to unplug him? It’s Marine’s decision,” said a National Rally elected representative. “It all depends on whether the proof is serious.”

But Bardella is no small player, and the National Rally’s opponents are hoping that the fallout of his possible resignation would damage Le Pen’s campaign durably.

Budget trouble

All of this comes just hours after Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s minority government introduced a 2027 budget with €43 billion worth of savings designed to reassure markets fretting about France’s massive debt and a stubbornly high budget deficit.

But without a parliamentary majority, getting lawmakers to agree to painful cuts will be tough, even if the specter of a potential financial crisis is starting to loom large. 

Borrowing cost have reached their highest levels since 2008 and the spread between French 10-year bonds and German ones — an indicator that measures investors’ appetite to hold French debt over more traditionally stable German debt — shot above 150 basis points on Friday, a level not seen in years.

One lawmaker from President Emmanuel Macron’s party Renaissance said he doesn’t see how the presidential hopefuls from the political center — former PMs Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal — will be spared the fallout.

“Every minute spent on the budget is a minute spent staring at our incapacity to get ourselves out of the mess,” the MP said.

Meanwhile, Mélenchon has called for his party officials to join more protests planned next Tuesday and protect pupils against alleged police violence. That could propel him to center stage, but it could also backfire if he is seen as taking part in the unrest.

Centrist MEP Sandro Gozi said the allegations against Bardella and the far left’s attitude to the protests “complicate the normalization strategy of the two sides.”

“Both Le Pen and Mélenchon are extremists who are far from fundamental Republican and European values,” Gozi said.

But as Macron’s term winds down, a sense is taking hold that France has been mismanaged and that parts of the country are falling apart.

It’s a perception any would-be successor with links to the current president will struggle to combat on the campaign trail.

Elisa Bertholomey and Sarah Paillou contributed reporting.

]]> en Polanski’s Greens look for their next opening https://www.politico.eu/article/polanskis-greens-look-for-their-next-opening/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:47:59 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9100286 BRIGHTON, England  — Green leader Zack Polanski has claimed credit for Andy Burnham’s recent arrival in No. 10. Now he’s trying to convince people that his party can still do more to move national politics.

In his second speech as head of the left-wing populist party — and less than a week before his personal brand is tested at the polls in Holborn and St Pancras, where he’s fighting to snag Keir Starmer’s recently vacated Westminster seat — Polanski positioned his party as a corrective, not a spoiler. 

“Vote Green, and watch Labour move,” was his message. “Between general elections, we change the government.” 

Polanski added: “Through our sustained pressure — and our historic wins — we have held the worst instincts of the Labour government in check. And started to move them in the right direction.” 

The Labour washout in May’s local elections, courtesy of voter defections to right-wing populist Reform UK as well as to the Greens, accelerated Starmer’s exit as prime minister over the summer. Burnham has since promised many of the things that under Starmer were within the Greens’ sole purview — public ownership, care, and housing. 

The task for the Green leader now is to decide where to push Labour next.

“It won’t surprise you to hear that I’m not hopeful about Labour’s backbone,” he told the crowd.

Hackney Mayor Zoë Garbett, who won her job in May’s local elections, said there were still “key differences” with the governing party, particularly on Gaza, climate and rent control — but conceded that Burnham had made it more difficult for the Green message. 

She said: “People were so fed up in May, they were done with people making promises and not delivering, but we need to put forward what our vision is as well, that’s what this conference and Zack’s speech is about.”

Then there’s North London

Walking on stage to Calvin Harris’ Let’s Go, Polanski’s galvanizing energy seemed to convince even some of the skeptics.

“He brought the fire,” said one Green activist on exiting the conference hall, “in a way they’re not really bringing the fire in Holborn.”

Campaigners have been fretting that the Greens haven’t done enough to “bring Burnham back down to earth.” One told POLITICO that next week’s vote would force the party to grapple with its failure to reckon with the new prime minister. 

Polanski’s speech went some way towards defining how he might do this. He went hard on rent caps, the proscription of Palestine Action, and new drilling in Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields. And in doing so, he took the first steps toward clarifying where the new battleground is. 

More in Common pollster Luke Tryl said that after being hit by the Burnham bounce and Polanski’s tumbling ratings, the Greens “need to make sure they don’t lose sight of the environment.” 

Polanski seems to agree. “Our differences with this Labour government could not be clearer,” he said in Brighton, “While they play politics with our planet — we stick to the science. While Andy Burnham barely whispers the word climate — we seek urgent action.” 

That was the one time Polanski mentioned the new prime minister’s name, as he joked that the outcome of the post-wildfire government COBRA meeting was to ban outdoor grills. 

The Green leader, currently a member of the London Assembly, also attacked Labour MPs for voting for the proscription of Palestine Action. 

“Our MPs didn’t troop through the yes lobby. Our MPs were cowed by fear or malicious attacks in the press. They stood up for the principles we hold so dear,” he said. 

Polanski is trying to position the party as the full-fat version of Burnham’s “end of neoliberalism” offering. This was set out in a strategy document earlier this summer, according to the Guardian,

“He is really speaking to what a lot of those disillusioned progressives wanted from Labour, and the reason why they left,” Tryl told POLITICO, arguing that the Greens should focus on the cost-of-living crisis and the environment as areas where they can claw back support. 

A “timid budget” would “offer the opportunity for the Greens to come back in,” he said. 

Tryl warned, however, about the “barnacles” on the party that may drive voters away, like a “Zionism is Racism” motion set to be debated Sunday. 

Amid those debates on whether the party takes on a more radical agenda, Tryl said: “The question for Greens is do you want to be a pressure group that is pushing Labour to the left, or do you want to beat them outright.”

]]> en 17 countries join forces to oppose EU budget cuts https://www.politico.eu/article/17-countries-join-forces-to-oppose-eu-budget-cuts/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 02 Oct 2026 14:39:01 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9098864 BRUSSELS — Seventeen EU governments have publicly warned against cuts to agriculture and regional payouts in the next seven-year budget, in a rebuke of Germany’s stance in the negotiations.

The letter — signed on Friday by Italy, Spain and Poland among others — heaps pressure on the Irish rotating presidency of the Council of the EU to leave untouched almost €900 billion of spending in the upcoming draft budget, which is expected to be presented next week.

This sets up tensions with a rival camp of six countries led by Germany, which renewed calls for cuts of several hundred billion euros across the board in a joint letter earlier this week.

“We therefore believe that the overall funding for Cohesion Policy and the CAP must be preserved in the next MFF,” the seventeen countries wrote in the letter to Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin seen by POLITICO.

The signatories include Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Romanian President Nicușor Dan coordinated the initiative and will host an informal meeting of those countries in the margins of the next European Council on Oct. 15 and 16.

The Multiannual Financial Framework, or MFF, finances everything from farmers’ subsidies to development aid, and is among the toughest negotiations in Brussels. In 2025, the European Commission proposed a budget of nearly €2 trillion for the 2028-2034 period and shifted hundreds of billions from agriculture and regional payouts, known as cohesion policy, to new priorities such as defense and competitiveness.  

The so-called Friends of Cohesion group warned that further reductions to agricultural and cohesion “would only weaken it [budget] and risk undermining public support for the European project.”

Ireland’s negotiating document, or negobox, will set the scene for discussions among the EU’s 27 leaders during the summit in Brussels in October.

EU governments are rushing to secure a final agreement among themselves by the end of the year, before national elections in France, Poland and Italy threaten to derail the negotiations.

One of the most sensitive issues involves introducing new EU-wide taxes, known as own resources, to finance the budget. The Commission proposed five new levies that are estimated to generate €66 billion per year.

The tax package is strongly supported by France, but individual proposals have been opposed by several national governments who fear that they will be disproportionately affected by the levies.

The 17 countries wrote in the letter that new own resources”should be genuine, fair, simple and non-regressive.”

To create more leeway, they also renewed calls to delay repayments of post-Covid debt that is expected to cost €25 billion per year and opposed budget discounts to wealthier countries, known as rebates.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:59:05 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.2 Brazil’s cliff‑hanger election could rob EU of key ally in Latin America https://euobserver.com/240911/brazils-cliffhanger-election-could-rob-eu-of-key-ally-in-latin-america/ Sat, 03 Oct 2026 10:29:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240911 Brussels watches on as one of the world's largest democracies heads to the polls on Sunday (4 September), with climate resiliance the Trump administration's influence in the Americas on the line.]]> Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the 80 year-old president of the world’s fifth largest country, is facing a tight race in a bid for his fourth presidential term in Brazil’s general elections on Sunday (4 October). The EU, which earlier this year concluded a landmark trade deal with the Mercosur bloc, which includes Brazil, will be watching the polls closely.

He holds a narrow poll lead over Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the country’s former president Jair, who is currently serving a 22 year prison sentence for staging a coup against Lula’s newly formed government in 2023.

The left-wing leader’s third term, won by with a slim 50.9 percent majority in 2022, distinguished itself for leading anti-deforestation policies and getting the EU-Mercosur trade partnership across its long-awaited finish line, 26 years after negotiations started.

Though Brussels suspended animal product imports from Brazil on 3 September, due to insufficient guarantees of antibiotic regulation compliance, “President von der Leyen commended President Lula’s role and political leadership in the negotiations leading up to the agreement,” the EU commission said in a statement.

Read more

MEPs approve ‘safeguards’ to halt cheap Mercosur imports if EU farmers suffer

The Mercosur deal marked a historic diversion of EU energies South of the Rio Grande river, at a time when Europe and Latin America were both being bombarded by tariff threats from Washington.

The Bolsonaros’ professed support of US president Donald Trump have critics worrying “this election could have major implications for the direction of Brazil’s foreign policy, its global influence,” wrote Dr. Christopher Sabatini, Latin America director at the Chatham house think tank.

Election interference by the US was discussed throughout Lula’s campaign, most notably with Meta disabling his Facebook ads just days before Brazilians went to cast their votes, state-run Agência Brasil reported on 25 September.

At a time when virtually every other democracy on the South American continent has pivoted to the right, a win for a Brazilian Trump enthusiast and supporter of environmental commodification would be a setback for the EU’s climate ambitions.

“A Flávio Bolsonaro government would represent a much stronger geopolitical alignment with Washington and the Trump administration. That could affect climate cooperation, deforestation policy, critical minerals and European access to Brazilian commodities and industrial partnerships,” said Eduardo Raguse, climate co-coordinator at NGO network Friends of the Earth Latin America.

Read more

Why young men are drawn to the far right and young women to the far left

Brazil’s climate observatory recorded its biggest annual fall in emissions in 15 years, with a 16.7 percent reduction in 2024 from the previous year, largely due to a drop in forest clearance in the Brazilian Amazon, which was halved over Lula’s third term.

But Lula has been simultaneously expanding Brazil’s national petrol company’s drilling area into the Amazon’s depths.

“Lula’s government has increasingly framed critical minerals as an issue of national sovereignty and industrial policy,” Raguse told EUobserver, since the Workers’ party leader has referred to Brazil’s petrol reserves as its “passport for the future.”

But along a global pivot to the right, a win for Bolsonaro’s heir or Lula’s renewed interest in fossil fuel politics would not stray too far from the EU’s current conservative climate script, and according to Socialist and Democrat MEP Leire Pajin, will mean little for EU trade.

“Whoever wins the election in Brazil, the EU-Mercosur relationship goes far beyond electoral cycles or trade,” the Spanish vice-president of the Euro-Latin American parliamentary assembly told EUobserver. “Governments may differ in priorities or pace, but the agreement transcends them.”

]]> [Interview] AI threatens to deepen gender gaps — unless women seize the tools, says computer expert https://euobserver.com/235901/interview-ai-threatens-to-deepen-gender-gaps-unless-women-seize-the-tools-says-computer-expert/ Sat, 03 Oct 2026 08:19:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=235901 From biased hiring algorithms to disappearing administrative posts, Bieliková argues that women risk being hit hardest by AI unless they seize the tools early and push for fairer, more accountable systems. ]]> Mária Bieliková began studying computer science before the World Wide Web was launched from CERN in 1989. She has lived through the development of programming from punch cards, which stored instructions for computers, to large language models, which allows almost anyone to write basic code.

Mária Bieliková founded the Kempelen Institute of Intelligent Technologies which she leads. She previously served as dean of the Faculty of Informatics and Information Technologies at the Slovak University of Technology in Bratislava.

Bieliková explained how artificial intelligence is set to affect women’s in the coming years.

“Studies predict women will be worse off in the labour market due to AI,” she said, while claiming such drawbacks also come with opportunities.

Do you think artificial intelligence can end humanity? And is that a tired question, or do you find it relevant?

This question needs to be answered patiently and sometimes with a smile, because nobody knows. Often it is just speculation, and there are many more immediate problems that we need to address.

It is true that AI is unlike other the technologies we have known so far and so were steam engines. But AI is fundamentally different. Still, I believe that if anything destroys us, it will be people. I am more afraid of those who use any technology carelessly, or those who do not take care to avoid hurting the planet. But I do not see a doomsday scenario where AI end the world. After all, our planet is very resilient.

AI research and development is largely in private hands. When you said you were afraid of people, did you mean specific individuals?

I did not mean specific people, but types of people who hold incredible power through technology and the data they hold about us. So for example, I fear for democracy. It is a system that evolved alongside society in a series of twists and turns since the days of ancient Greece, and we have come a long way since then. Democracy still has weaknesses, but so far we have not devised a better tool.

Yet the ability of AI to influence elections undermines a fundamental principle of democracy. Data administrators who nobody elected have suddenly become very powerful. And elected officials often follow and support tech titans. Technology is transforming geopolitics, and this could have serious consequence concerning us all; these are not mere political games played by those in power.

Experts warn that disinformation campaigns and deepfake videos generated by artificial intelligence, which can be easily made, will flood our online spaces. What can individuals do about this?

If I knew what an individual could do to resolve these problems, I would go and do it. But action should come from both the government and individual.

But we should not rely on someone at the top to change everything. Indeed, we determine the outcome of elections, but the major problem is we are being influenced and manipulated in entirely new ways. And many politicians lack the will to protect us from that. The only way to prevent being manipulated is for us as individuals to inform ourselves.

In the past, when someone said something publicly, we usually believed it. It is uncomfortable, but we will have to change how we trust. We cannot believe things automatically; we must demand trustworthy sources for every claim.

A good place to look is towards media outlets that we know verify information diligently – a layman cannot do so with all information they stumble upon.

Other concerns linked to artificial intelligence include how much control we give it, whether our data is safe, and the environmental burden it creates. Are there other “landmines” ordinary people have not noticed?

We live in a society where we cannot trust everyone. Human nature is such that, say, 90 percent of people consciously or subconsciously act in their own interest. I do not mean to condone stealing or cheating, of course, but it is clear to me that people will act in their own interest.

This brings me again to democracy, a vital tool which needs to be protected. Without checks and balances, which AI can undermine, democracy is at risk.

The last thing I asked a chatbot was what I should pack on holiday. Do you ever talk to them about everyday matters, or do you avoid this so as to avoid sharing data about yourself?

Why Magyar picked a fight with Kyiv over the ‘Carpathian Eight’ https://euobserver.com/240579/orbanism-without-orban-why-magyar-picked-a-fight-with-kyiv-over-the-carpathian-eight/ Sat, 03 Oct 2026 06:24:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240579 Some expected a change in Hungary's pro-Russian foreign policy after Viktor Orbán’s fall. But they failed to take into account the domestic political pressures on Hungary's PM .]]> Some expected a change in Hungary’s pro-Russian foreign policy after Viktor Orbán’s fall. But they failed to take into account the domestic political pressures on Hungary’s prime minister Péter Magyar.

An unexpected source of tension in Ukrainian-Hungarian relations came at a meeting of the newly formed ‘Carpathian Eight’ (C8) in late September. At the meeting in Kyiv, PM Magyar was embroiled in a sharp exchange with Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha, who criticised Budapest for not taking part.

Magyar responded to Sybiha by claiming that Hungary had been included in the C8 without his consent.

“To claim that a sovereign country is a member of an international cooperation (Carpathian Integration) without prior consultation or consent of the country concerned is completely unacceptable,” Magyar said on social media.

This comes after Hungary-Ukraine relations began to improve rapidly following the formation of the Tisza government in May.

Under Orbán’s government, relations had fallen to a historic low, raising the prospect of escalation. In June, Magyar announced that he had reached an agreement with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky on settling the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia, hailing it as a historic deal.

Since June, however, Hungary has repeatedly blocked Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations, arguing that progress on settling the rights of Hungarians in Transcarpathia has fallen short of expectations.

Orbán’s Fidesz party previously used the same argument to block Ukraine’s integration efforts.

Three months after the so-called historic agreement, Ukraine’s foreign minister Sybiha wrote that although Orbán had lost the election, Orbánism (a policy based on isolation and obstruction) prevailed in Hungary.

“Orbanism has done no good, neither to Hungary nor to the broader region, in the past — and it will not do anyone any good moving forward,” said Sybiha on social media.

Domestic Hungarian politics can explain the dispute.

Read more

Orbán era is over, as Tisza scores historic victory in Hungary

MOL, an oil company, signed a memorandum with Ukraine’s Naftogaz at the C8 meeting on the possible establishment of Ukrainian oil storage facilities in Hungary.

The deal was criticised by Fidesz politicians, and Magyar’s government strongly distanced itself from the deal, too. Fidesz may have contributed to Magyar entering the dispute over C8 participation so very forcefully.

What is the Carpathian Eight?

In August, Zelensky announced the creation of the C8 to bring together countries from the wider Carpathian border region. The Ukrainian president said its members would focus primarily on the economy, security, the environment and investment.

Ukraine described it as a project intended to strengthen cross-border cooperation even with countries that do not provide it with military aid. Alongside Ukraine were to be Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, Czechia, Austria and Hungary.

Michal Lebduška, an analyst at the Association for International Affairs in Prague (AMO), said that it was one of many regional initiatives. While he did not believe it would trigger “major cooperation”, it could nevertheless be important.

The inaugural summit of the newly formed C8 was held last month (18 September) in Bukovel, in the Ivano-Frankivsk region, around 160 km from both the Slovak and Hungarian borders. Zelensky called it “an important beginning” and thanked the countries of the Carpathian region for being among Kyiv’s most reliable allies.

From Ukraine’s perspective, however, the meeting had mixed results. On the one hand, several leaders travelled to Bukovel in person, lending the gathering greater diplomatic weight. Polish PM Donald Tusk, Romanian president Nicușor Dan and Serbian president Aleksandar Vučić all attended in person.

On the other hand, the remaining countries sent lower-ranking representatives. Slovakia’s PM Robert Fico had initially indicated that he would attend, and was originally due to meet Tusk. At the last minute, however, he announced that he could not attend the summit due to sudden illness.

Slovakia was ultimately represented by Marek Eštok, state secretary at the foreign ministry.

Andrej Babiš’s Czech government all but completely ignored the initiative. As Respekt magazine wrote, Babiš declined the opportunity to visit Ukraine and did not send any representative to Bukovel.

So Czechia was represented at the summit only by opposition deputy Senate president Jiří Drahoš.

And Austria was ultimately represented by Christine Schwarz-Fuchs, president of the Federal Council.

Hungary sent Ádám Ceglédi, the acting chargé d’affaires at the Hungarian embassy in Kyiv, as the Hungarian foreign ministry confirmed to Telex.

Ukraine expected stronger support

“There are many different forms of cooperation in this region: the Visegrád Four, the Slavkov format and the Central European Initiative. Ukraine is interested in improving its relations with some countries,” Péter Techet, a foreign-policy analyst and researcher at the Institute for Danube Region and Central Europe in Vienna, said.

According to the analyst, Ukraine may have hoped that Orbán’s fall would bring a clear shift in Hungary’s Ukraine policy. Anita Orbán, as foreign minister, has confirmed this by pursuing a foreign policy moving away from Russia.

However, Ukrainians did not take Magyar’s domestic political interests into account.

]]> G7 releases diesel stocks after Trump pressure, EU denies caving https://euobserver.com/240914/g7-releases-diesel-stocks-after-trump-pressure-eu-denies-caving/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:59:05 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240914 G7 leaders agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of emergency oil and fuel stocks after weeks in which Washington pressed European capitals to open their diesel reserves. Brussels said US threats played no part.]]> The EU and its G7 partners agreed on Friday (2 October) to a coordinated release of 100 million barrels of diesel and crude through the International Energy Agency (IEA) over four months.

The release includes “a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days,” a press brief released after a Friday afternoon call read.

The call was initiated by French president Emmanuel Macron who holds the rotating G7 presidency on Friday, after he spoke to US president Donald Trump on Thursday.

“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately,” Trump wrote on Truth Social shortly afterwards.

Trump had pressured EU leaders to agree to the release all week.

On Thursday, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent urged Europe to “immediately” tap its reserves.

And EU leaders had received a proposal from the White Housethe same day for 120 million barrels of diesel over 180 days.

Washington had already approached France, Germany, Italy, Ireland and the UK individually, warning they could face US diesel export bans if they did not comply.

US diesel prices hit a record $6.53 per gallon last week, which is a liability for Trump’s Republicans ahead of the 3 November midterm elections.

Europe’s reward is a single line in the G7 statement, which reaffirms a commitment “to refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products” between G7 countries.

The EU also on Friday had insisted that any further release come with a US pledge to avoid a unilateral diesel ban, and rejected the suggestion that they buckled to US pressure.

“We fully reject a [US] ban on diesel. A ban would not be beneficial to anyone. It would undermine our trust in the US as a reliable partner,” said Anna-Kaisa Itkonen, the commission’s energy spokesperson.

She declined to comment on the leader’s call ahead of time.

Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho said the coordination had “nothing to do with” recent threats.

She noted that gas prices had risen by 140 percent and diesel prices had doubled since February, and that a release agreed in March was still being implemented.

The G7 text presented Friday’s decision to release the 100 million barrels as continuing those commitments.

But the commission’s own oil coordination group concluded this week that there was “no immediate security supply issue” in the EU, Itkonen said.

Emergency stocks exist to deal with supply disruptions, not prices.

But the IEA route gives European capitals political cover, allowing them to present the release as collective action rather than a concession to Washington.

And it may not be the last one. “We will convene in the context of the IEA in the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary,” the G7 statement said.

]]> The war changes yet again: Ukrainians use domestic missile for first time as Russians launch assault on bridges (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,681) https://euobserver.com/240876/the-war-changes-yet-again-ukrainians-use-domestic-missile-for-first-time-as-russians-launch-assault-on-bridges-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1681/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 16:29:22 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240876 A defence analyst warned that Russia is mass-producing "thousands" of new drones “far more dangerous and faster" than jet-powered Shaheds which Ukraine cannot yet stop.]]>
  • In a sign of humble progress, the FP-7 ballistic missile saw its first deployment.
  • Russian forces are now attacking Kyiv’s bridges.
  • No resolution to jet-powered Geran drones with new threat is on the horizon.
  • Ukraine lost another MiG-29 and its pilot, while Russia has lost a Mi-8 helicopter with a crew of three.
  • Videos of the day: attacks on a bridge in Kyiv; a drone struck a school full of children and teachers; a ground drone recorded the impact of two glide bombs.

    • FP-7 ballistic missile made in Ukraine were deployed for the first time. This is progress, but one should not expect miracles.

    “Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat deployment. Thank you for the results. Next step: serial production. Glory to Ukraine!” With these words and a short video, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky announced a long-awaited milestone in Ukraine’s arms programme. The next step is expected to be the deployment of the larger and more dangerous FP-9 missile.

    For now, however, this was only its first deployment against an unknown target, with an unknown outcome. The Russian analytical channel Military Informant did not rule out the possibility of the footage being recorded at a training ground with the intention to deflect criticism of Fire Point, the Kyiv-based manufacturer whose production is behind schedule.

    The FP-7 missile is an interesting technical achievement that could expand the Ukrainian army’s ability to strike important targets. Expectations should be kept low. This is because the missile has not yet entered serial production its specifications lag behind those of Russia’s short-range Iskander missiles.

    The FP-7 is based on the Soviet-origin 48N6 surface-to-air missile, used in some versions of the S-300 system and still deployed by Russia in the more modern S-400. A Ukrainian outlet says that the FP-7 has an estimated range of only 200 km and a warhead weighing up to 150 kg.

    Russia’s Iskander missiles weighs more than twice as much, and Russia has already used a version with an extended range well beyond 500 km. The Ukrainian FP-7’s use will therefore be limited to areas up to roughly 100 km from the front line. It is certainly not a means for strategic strikes against Russian industry deep inside enemy lines.

    Ukraine could strike further with a FP-9 missile, and developing them remains a goal to work towards. The two types of missile differ significantly. They were analysed in August by the Russian Telegram channel Russian Engineer. The FP-7 is smaller and the FP-9 larger. Its maximum range is estimated at 855 km (far enough to reach Moscow,) its warhead is expected to weigh up to 800 kg.

    The outlet focusing on the war’s technical parameters compared the Iskander with the FP-9:

    “The 9M723 Iskander-M missile has a diameter of 920 mm, while the FP-9’s is 1,100 mm. The missiles are 7.2 and 9.5 metres long. The solid-fuel rocket motor is approximately 4.2 metres long in the 9M723 and 6.5 metres in the FP-9. Fuel mass is estimated at 2.6 and five tonnes. With a warhead weighing around 500 kg, calculations indicate ranges of up to 500 km and 1,000+ km. If the warhead weighs around 800 kg, the range will be approximately 800 km.”

    The media’s performance estimate therefore matches official Ukrainian data.

    According to the Russian Engineer Telegram channel, the FP-9 is conceptually based on the Iskander and builds on the Ukrainian Sapsan project, which was never brought to the final stage.

    The Ukrainians displayed both missiles at a trade fair in Denmark in August, where the following photographs were also taken:

    The Russians have started attacking Kyiv’s bridges. This fulfils the wishes of Russian pro-war hawks, who for years have complained that bridges in the capital of the invaded country were still standing.

    But Syria is also no longer the single biggest source of asylum claims after the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime 22 months ago, a factor that appears to have been conveniently ignored.

    On Thursday, he told reporters after a meeting of EU interior ministers in Luxembourg that irregular arrivals have dropped 55 percent in the past two years.

    “So that’s a record low in the asylum applications,” said the former Austrian finance minister, adding that Austria and Sweden have recorded equally low asylum numbers and that Germany is deporting more people than are asking for protection.

    “The basis for all of that, and the foundation for all of that, is the pact, the pact on migration and asylum,” he said, in comments that were echoed by Ireland’s migration minister, Jim O’Callaghan.

    The pact, spanning a mix of complex regulations, was launched in June. Despite having two years to prepare for the launch, its implementation remains patchy.

    An investigation by the left-leaning outlet Mediapart said on Thursday (1 October) that it could authenticate antisemitic messages from 2013 and attribute them to Bardella.

    In the messages, Bardella, an MEP and chair of the far-right Patriots for Europe group, said “all the banks are owned by Jews” and that Israel aims to create a new world order. Earlier media reports also found his secret Twitter account publishing racist content, such as mocking a young Black man who had suffered police violence.

    He denied having written the messages, calling the evidence “crude montages” and “obscure screenshots that can easily be manipulated,”  he wrote on social media, adding he would sue Mediapart for defamation.

    “Either Mediapart is running this operation itself, or it is being manipulated by interested parties,” he has said.

    ]]>         Magyar waives his own immunity, as Hungary targets billions in alleged fraud and two former Orbán ministers in custody (Day 143 of the Tisza government) https://euobserver.com/240728/magyar-waives-his-own-immunity-as-hungary-targets-billions-in-alleged-fraud-and-two-former-orban-ministers-in-custody-day-143-of-the-tisza-government/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 11:38:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240728 PM Peter Magyar waives his own immunity as Hungary's "Operation Purgatory" saw authorities detain two former Orbán ministers over alleged multibillion-forint corruption. The new asset recovery office took over four major cases, including Orbán's brother's visa business, while Hungary may soon join the European Public Prosecutor's Office.]]> More than a year ago, we launched our Hungary Briefing, a weekly round-up of the election campaign. Since the historic vote in April to remove Viktor Orbán, the series has followed the new Tisza government and its first moves in office. This week’s topics:

    ]]>         Europe’s Affordable Housing Act must look beyond short-term rentals https://euobserver.com/240606/europes-affordable-housing-act-must-look-beyond-short-term-rentals/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 08:35:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240606 As Brussels pins its housing fix on curbing Airbnb-style rentals, campaigners warn lawmakers are ducking a far bigger fight over Europe’s millions of empty homes and the people still sleeping rough.]]> The appointment of a dedicated Commissioner for Energy and Housing, the launch of the European Affordable Housing Plan, and growing political attention to Europe’s housing crisis raised expectations of a comprehensive policy response.

    The next legislative step was therefore expected to address one of the Union’s most pressing social challenges. The proposed Affordable Housing Act is an important step in that direction. Yet its binding Regulation focuses primarily on one specific aspect of the problem: restrictions on non-primary housing use, particularly short-term rentals, in areas under housing stress.

    While addressing short-term rentals is a welcome intention, it cannot on its own provide a comprehensive response to Europe’s housing crisis. 

    The pressure that holiday homes and short-term rental platforms are putting on housing markets, particularly in popular tourist destinations, has been rising, and giving local authorities better tools to respond is important. However, questions have already been raised about whether the proposed framework will give cities sufficient room to act effectively.

    For instance, the proposed approach to defining “areas under housing stress” risks being too narrow. Housing stress cannot be understood through property prices, income levels and short-term projections alone. Energy poverty, combined housing and energy costs, overcrowding, vacancy rates and the condition of existing housing stock all influence whether households can access decent and affordable homes. A broader understanding of housing stress would better reflect the reality facing communities across Europe.

    Yet the broader picture reveals an important limitation: many of the structural drivers of housing unaffordability remain outside the scope of the binding Regulation. In particular, it gives limited attention to one of Europe’s most significant untapped housing resources: the buildings and homes that already exist.

    Renovation, adaptive re-use and the mobilisation of vacant and underused buildings feature in the European Affordable Housing Plan and the Recommendation accompanying the Act. But if Europe is serious about increasing affordable housing stock, these approaches should play a stronger role in the framework itself.

    Across the EU, more than 47 million dwellings are estimated to be unoccupied. This does not mean that every empty home can or should be brought back into use. But it illustrates the scale of an existing resource that cannot be ignored. Bringing even a fraction of suitable vacant and underused stock back into use could create much-needed homes while reducing pressure for new construction and making better use of existing buildings and infrastructure.

    Europe cannot reuse buildings it cannot see. Yet many public authorities still lack reliable information about which homes and buildings are vacant, why they are empty, what condition they are in and what potential they have for affordable housing.

    The EU does not need to start from scratch. The Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) and National Building Renovation Plans already provide a natural policy framework for understanding and planning the future of Europe’s building stock. Vacancy identification, mapping and monitoring should become part of the binding architecture of the Affordable Housing Act, ensuring that public authorities are, at a minimum, equipped to identify vacant and underused homes and assess their potential for conversion into decent and affordable homes.

    Identifying vacant buildings, however, is only the first step. The accompanying Recommendation could go further by providing guidance on how to mobilise vacant properties, support the conversion of different building types and develop viable financing models.

    EU financing should also better support the mobilisation and re-use of existing buildings. The next EU budget should continue to support affordable housing investment and recognise that renovation and re-use projects simultaneously deliver social, climate and energy benefits.

    Ultimately, however, success cannot be measured only in buildings renovated or investment mobilised. It must be measured in whether people can access decent homes they can afford.

    According to the Commission’s EU Anti-Poverty Strategy, one in five Europeans – nearly 93 million people – are at risk of poverty or social exclusion, while approximately 1 million people experience homelessness. Affordable housing policy must therefore place particular emphasis on those least well served by the housing market, including lower-income households and people experiencing or at risk of housing exclusion.

    The Affordable Housing Act is an important step forward. But as it moves through the legislative process, there is still an opportunity to broaden its ambition. A stronger focus on re-use, better implementation support, dedicated financing and a more people-centred approach would help turn a useful regulatory framework into a more comprehensive response to Europe’s housing affordability challenge.

    Italy brought back border controls with Spain in August, and has now extended them until at least 15 October. Giorgia Meloni’s government fears that migrants who arrived in Ceuta, reach the continent and Italy.

    Are these restrictions legal in the Schengen area? What are the EU’s levies to avoid such controls?

    Since 1 August, Italy has temporarily reintroduced controls at its air and sea borders with Spain. The measure has now been extended until 15 October. In return, Spain has also introduced controls at its air and sea borders with Italy.

    The starting point was the arrival of tens of thousands of migrants in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July. Italy said it was concerned about possible secondary movements towards the rest of Europe, and brought back controls at its borders with Spain.

    But from a legal point of view, EU countries can’t simply reintroduce border controls whenever they want.

    The Schengen area is based on the principle of free movement, meaning there should normally be no checks at internal borders. The Schengen Borders Code provides an exception. If a country faces a serious threat to public policy or internal security, it can temporarily reintroduce border controls, as a measure of last resort.

    The controls can initially be introduced for up to 30 days, and can then be extended under certain conditions.

    Italy has already extended its measure, which has now been in place for more than two months.

    What does the European Commission say about Italy’s decision? The Commission has been asked about the Italian controls and says it is currently assessing the situation.

    But the Brussels-based organisation The Good Lobby argues that Italy is violating the Schengen rules. It filed a complaint with the European Commission, asking it to open an infringement procedure against Italy.

    According to Alberto Alemanno, who filed the complaint, there is no security threat that would justify bringing back the controls.

    His argument is that none of the migrants who arrived in Ceuta were transferred to Italy. And, he says, people travelling between Ceuta and mainland Spain are already subject to identity checks.

    So Italy’s justification, he argues, does not meet the conditions set out in the Schengen Borders Code.

    Now, is Italy the only EU country bringing back border controls? No. If you look at the notifications sent by EU countries to the European Commission, around ten countries have reported temporary controls at some of their internal borders in recent months.

    Read more

    In response to the situation in Ceuta, Italy is the main example.

    Austria also notified the Commission of controls in September, citing the situation in Ceuta among several reasons. But those controls concern its land borders with Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovenia.

    So Austria is not checking passengers arriving by air from Spain.

    Germany, for example, has invoked the same exception in the Schengen rules to carry out controls at its land borders with all its neighbours.

    That does not mean that every border crossing is closed, or that every traveller is systematically checked. It means German authorities can carry out checks at those borders, including spot checks.

    Those measures include the new Migration and Asylum Pact and new rules on entry and border management. The bigger question, then, is how long temporary border controls can remain in place before they stop being an exception to Schengen and become the new normal.

The law states clearly that you can do what you want at home, but if you work in the public sector you must refrain from displaying your religion. There are laws covering this, and there is absolutely no need to devise new ones. Le Pen’s ideas in this regard seem to be mere campaign slogans; we cannot take them literally.

    Read more

    Islamic veil can be banned in workplace, says EU court

    Yet, a major Le Monde poll shows the French are more concerned about the economy than immigration. Immigration ranks fourth, after social issues and ecology.

    That is true, but other polls show that, for many voters, the issues of migration and safety overlap considerably.

    So, as concerns about security become increasingly prominent, people are more concerned about security and often link it to migration. Marine Le Pen will certainly try to make it one of the key issues, alongside the economy.

    Donald Trump is betting on voluntary commitments from AI companies. On Tuesday (29 September), he unveiled a self-regulatory agreement drawn up with some of the biggest names in the AI industry.

    What does it mean, and how does it differ from the EU’s Code of Practice for general-purpose AI?

    On Tuesday, September 29, Trump brought together the CEOs of some of the biggest AI companies. Together, they signed what could be described as a self-regulation pact: a short list of non-binding commitments called the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

    That’s the other novelty: Trump no longer wants to talk about artificial intelligence, but about “super intelligence”. The term AI apparently has negative connotations.

    So, what exactly have these companies committed to? The CEOs of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, SpaceX and Nvidia have pledged to put safeguards in place, quickly detect and fix problems, and have their systems checked by independent auditors.

    The principle of voluntary commitments may sound familiar to Europeans: They echo the EU’s Code of Practice for general-purpose AI — which, like the White House agreement, is not legally binding.

    So what’s the difference? First of all, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have also signed the EU code, while Meta, SpaceX and Nvidia have not.

    And, more importantly, the EU does have binding rules in place: the AI Act, which is already in force. As part of this regulation, the European Commission developed the Code of Practice to help companies comply with the rules.

    You could think of it as a checklist for AI companies, to help them make sure they are complying with the law.

    Read more

    Let’s not allow AI firms to use fears of future dystopias to distract Europeans from existing problems

    Another difference is the sheer volume of recommendations. The document published by Trump is just one page long. The European Code of Practice runs to more than 60 pages and was prepared with the help of dozens of independent experts.

    It is also more comprehensive, covering not only safety, but also transparency and copyright. But this raises another question: if both documents are voluntary,  how effective can they actually be?

    When the European Code of Practice was published, some civil society organisations criticised it, arguing that voluntary commitments are not enough and that concrete obligations are needed.

    Read more

    EU states urged to ‘go beyond’ AI Act to protect people from abusive surveillance

    There are binding obligations under the AI Act. But they are not as precise as what is in the code of conduct.

    Similar criticisms have emerged since the White House agreement was published on Tuesday. And it is worse in the US case, since companies are absolutely not legally bound by the commitments they have made.

    The United States has generally been less inclined towards binding regulation of the sector. Trump has argued that rules can hinder the development of companies, and has promoted a national framework that is as minimally restrictive as possible.

    The White House document does leave the door open to legislation in the future. It says that, over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into lows or regulations.

    But for now, they remain voluntary commitments. If you are interested in this topic, there will be a live event on Tuesday next week about AI and its safeguards, organised by VoxEurope.

    Beyond agriculture, Ukraine’s pharmaceutical industry could offer the EU an opportunity to reduce its reliance on imports of generic medicines from China and various Asian countries. Thanks to its favourable climate, Ukraine also has great potential for various types of renewable energy.

    ]]>         Europe’s children will inherit public-health crisis from new EU pesticide approvals https://euobserver.com/240266/europes-children-will-inherit-public-health-crisis-from-new-eu-pesticide-approvals/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 09:37:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240266 By extending pesticide approvals and keeping hazardous products on the market, Brussels is bending to Big Pharma and causing a food-system and public-health burden for decades to come.]]> The European Union once prided itself on leading the world in protecting children. Today, policymakers backed by big polluters are betraying that promise in the name of “competitiveness”. 

    In June 2026, Florence, Franck, and Isabelle packed their bags and headed to Brussels. Why? Because their children have all suffered serious harm from pesticides. 

    These children have endured physical pain and heavy medical procedures, including repeated chemotherapy treatments. And their families have shouldered both the financial and emotional burdens alongside them.

    As Isabelle puts it: “It destroys a family.” Her own daughter has been fighting leukaemia for the last seven years.

    And they are not alone. In 2024, almost one in 20 children in the EU were exposed to dangerous levels of pesticides; that’s 380,000 kids. Now these parents have a clear message for policymakers: prioritise public health and stop dismantling the rules that protect children against harmful substances. 

    In 2024, around 316,000 tonnes of toxic pesticides were sold in the EU to be sprayed across our countryside, risking not only the health of farmers but also polluting our soil, air and water.  

    The European Environment Agency in Copenhagen has reported environmentally unsafe levels of pesticides in about a quarter of Europe’s rivers. In groundwater – which supplies 65 percent of the water we drink in Europe – unsafe levels were detected in 11-18 percent of water bodies. 

    In the same year, trifluoroacetic acid, a harmful “forever chemical” that forms when ‘PFAS’ pesticides and F-gases break down, showed up in 94 percent of drinking water samples tested across 11 EU countries. 

    We are surrounded by pesticide pollution. It’s even in our homes. 

    But what’s happening in Brussels?

    In December 2025, the European Commission proposed a legislative package that would remove fundamental environmental and health protections against pesticides in the EU.

    Among other changes, the proposal – ironically labelled the ‘Food and Feed Safety’ Omnibus – suggests extending pesticide approvals indefinitely and relaxing the rules to allow pesticides already identified as hazardous to remain on the EU market. 

    Let that sink in, no pun intended.

    These proposals are a political choice to prioritise short-term profits for Big Polluters over children’s lives, people’s health, and the nature and ecosystems we need to survive.

    Human health is at stake, and children are at particular risk – as they absorb substances more easily and are less able to excrete them. 

    Pesticide exposure is linked to the development of childhood cancers, hormone disruption, neurodevelopmental impairments and birth defects. And prenatal and early childhood exposure can permanently alter development, with consequences that can be irreversible – and deadly.  

    Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, as well as the UN-declared human right to a healthy environment, all EU countries must commit to protecting children from environmental harm and ensure the highest attainable standard of health.

    These principles must guide the work of EU institutions. 

    Yet, instead of strengthening protections, the EU is moving backwards at a worrying speed. This is largely due to intense (and repeated) lobbying from multi-billion euro corporations, which includes the pesticides industry. Corporate chemical giants now spend €46m a year just to lobby the EU; that’s over 60 percent more than in 2020. 

    Make it make sense

    The incoherence of current EU policy is troubling. On the one hand, the EU Commission is celebrating its new Intergenerational Fairness Strategy – a framework that is meant to ensure today’s policies do not disadvantage future generations. On the other, the same institution is actively seeking to relax controls of harmful substances. 

    Ripping up rules that protect people and the planet only benefits Big Polluters, industries that already make billions in profits at the expense of children’s health.

    What’s more, an independent assessment found that the measures the EU institutions propose “will not accelerate innovations and authorisations”. In short, these proposals would actually make Europe less competitive.

    Children’s rights and youth organisations have warned that deregulation exposes children to serious (and preventable) health risks. And the international scientific community recently stressed that robust environmental risk assessments cannot be optional.

    Ultimately, Europe should widen and accelerate its access to pesticide-free alternatives. It must also support farmers in their efforts to transition away from pesticides, towards a more sustainable and resilient model.

    So, what can be done? First, the EU must close the tap on pesticide use and production, and support farmers transitioning to safer alternatives. Second, it’s time for leaders to hold Big Polluters accountable for the damage they cause – not force the bill onto regular taxpayers and families harmed by these toxic substances.

    Florence, Franck, and Isabelle’s children are among the hundreds of thousands already affected by pesticides. And they show that victims of pesticides are not just a statistic.

    The ‘Food and Feed Safety Omnibus’ raises fundamental questions. Who exactly is the EU’s food policy supposed to protect? How many more children need to be harmed for politicians to act? And what kind of future do EU institutions want to build? 

    Should pesticide protections be treated as obstacles to short-term profits, or should children be able to grow up safely? 

    Politicians should reject this devastating Omnibus proposal and work instead to support the EU’s transition to safe, sustainable, and resilient farming.

Instead, the employment agency that arranged her job had quietly enrolled her in school.

    She discovered this only after translating the papers she had been given. One said she was a student at an adult secondary school in Sieradz, another enrolled her at a Polish university. But Maria had never applied to either institution, attended a class or even heard of them.

    Her case is part of a wider trade in fake student documents that exploited Poland’s labour and immigration systems. Employment agencies used fictitious student status to make foreign workers cheaper to employ, while private universities issued certificates that could help foreigners obtain visas or legalise their stay.

    An investigation by the Polish publication Onet found the same schools and universities repeatedly appearing in documents issued to foreign workers from around the world. Some institutions existed largely on paper; in other cases, fraudsters forged documents in the names of legitimate schools without their knowledge.

    The schemes went beyond fake student cards. Private universities also issued certificates used to obtain visas, enter the Schengen area or legalise residency.

    They cost Poland’s social-security system millions of zloty and left some migrants facing job losses, residency problems and possible deportation – while people linked to the schools have established ties to Poland’s pro-Russian organisations and media.

    Read more

    EU’s new cross‑border work rules favour recruitment, not workers, say critics

    Fake students cheaper for employers

    Polish labour laws incentivise employment of students aged up to 26 under so-called agreements to perform a job. It means employers do not have to pay social security or health insurance contributions for them. The workers cost less than regular employees.

    So, student status has become a sought-after commodity that employment agencies have exploited for gains.

    A central figure in the case is Dariusz M., a school head in Sieradz detained by police in late May. When reporters from TVN24 posed as employers looking for a way to legalise the employment of foreign immigrants, M. offered to enrol them as students for 750 zloty (around €175) per person.

    Prosecutors suspect him of participating in an organised group that allegedly issued around 2,500 false study certificates, costing the Polish state nearly six million zloty (more than €1.4m) in unpaid contributions.

    Documents were often arranged by employment agencies with foreign workers unaware they had formally been enrolled at a school.

    “In most cases, they do not even know they are involved in something illegal. They trust the employment agency,” said Rocio Flores, president of the Union of Latin American Workers in Poland.

    When an inspection uncovers the fraud, the foreign workers face losing their jobs, residency problems and, in some cases, deportation. “We migrants suffer most as a result,” Flores said.

    Inspections carried out by Poland’s social insurance authority confirmed there were many such cases.

    In August, Dziennik Gazeta Prawna reported that Poland’s social insurance body (ZUS) stepped up inspections of companies employing foreigners with pupil or student status.

    They reported that inspectors uncovered cases in which agencies pay schools for fake study certificates despite the worker having never attended classes, with Poland’s social welfare system losing out on millions of zloty.

    Schools oblivious to study scam

    Not all paperwork for fake students came from education institutions themselves. Some student cards and study certificates were forged in the name of real schools without their knowledge, as was the case of a Cosinus network branch in the town of Piaseczno.

    Its head, Elżbieta Gotchold-Leśniewski, showed Onet reporters a file containing 62 forgeries found in various parts of Poland and had been issued to people from South America, Africa, Asia and Europe. “That is not my signature, and the school’s hologram is wrong too. In fact, many things are wrong,” she said.

    Read more

    Von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech risks making border pushbacks ‘normal’ EU migration policy

    The forgers incorrectly copied the four-leaf clover in the school’s logo, giving rise to the term “fake four-leaf clovers” in the Polish website’s headline. The documents were nevertheless convincing enough to be accepted by employers or used by holders during ticket inspections on public transport.

    A student card and certificate package cost 200 to 800 zloty (€45 to €180). One man called the school directly because he had paid 600 (€140) zloty for a set of documents and wanted to know when classes would begin. The school’s staff told him he was, in fact, not registered there at all.

    Dodgy paperwork for 20+ nationalities

    Since 2022, Poland’s border guard has been investigating a group that, under the cover of three private universities, sold foreigners documents needed to obtain visas or legalise their stays.
