Faltering demand, especially in the USA, has promoted concerns about oversupply and the prospect of another whisk(e)y loch. A number of Scotch distillers are slowing down production, but for Tom Bruce-Gardyne it feels like a bigger issue across the pond …

“Every drop of liquid we distil, every barrel we choose to fill, every palate that we make and move around the world has to work harder for returns on our capital.” This was the solemn pledge of Ewan Andrew, Diageo’s President Global Supply Chain & Procurement, at the company’s Capital Markets Day presentation that followed its full-year results on August 6th.

The current value of Diageo’s maturing stocks is put at $8.5bn, of which around two thirds is Scotch whisky. That represents a huge stash of casks slumbering in warehouses across Scotland, feeding the angels up above, and not exactly working hard. 

Ewan describes Diageo’s inventory as “a sizeable competitive advantage if it is deployed correctly.” But it seems it has grown too big. “We have scaled back production and distillation,” he told analysts at the presentation. “That’s been done across Scotch, North American whiskey and Tequila. We are at the minimum requirements for future blend and support of growth.” 

Judging by one of the graphs he displayed, there is to be a dramatic cut in production of about two thirds in this fiscal year, before a partial recovery through to FY29. In his words, compared to the past three years: “we are reducing our barrel by more than 50 per cent in the forward three-year cycle.”

How these cuts will fall between Scotch, North American whiskey and Tequila is unclear. We know that Diageo paused production at its third biggest malt distillery of Teaninich that has a 10m litre capacity last September, and did the same to its Roseisle maltings in November. Production at the company’s massive Cameronbridge grain distillery has also been reduced, leading to eight job cuts which has provoked the workers to go on strike. 

Paddy Fletcher, co-founder of the Port of Leith distillery, believes these production cuts are really to appease City investors who struggle to grasp the long-term nature of the industry, and are demanding that Diageo look at its free cash-flow metrics. “The only way to reduce your free cash-flow, is to stop making whisky,” he says. 

“But you’ll find in the background a couple of guys working in the supply chain screaming ‘Please, don’t do this to us again, because every ten years you do the same thing, and in five years’ time you’ll come back and say ‘Where’s the whisky? I’ve got massive growing demand’.” 

Whisky producers cutting back

Time will tell, but it’s fair to say that Diageo is not the only Scotch producer cutting back. The independent whisky firm of Ian Macleod Distillers lowered production at its Glengoyne and Rosebank distilleries by 30 per cent this year, while there have intermittent pauses at LVMH’s Glenmorangie distillery and at Brown Forman’s Glenglassaugh and Benriach distilleries.

Brown Forman, famous for Jack Daniel’s, is well aware of the oversupply of American whiskey. The state of Kentucky is drowning in bourbon with 16.2m barrels in its warehouses at the start of the year, compared to less than 6m a decade ago. 

Much of the reason for these vast stocks can be put down to speculation. Prospectors were lured in by the promise of quick returns. It was said you could fill a barrel for $750 and flog it for $4,000 four years later to someone who would bottle it up and sell it on. There was no brand or market in sight from the outset, and in the end, there were no buyers either.

There was a similar if somewhat smaller, whiskey ‘Gold Rush’ in Ireland where the speculators have since vanished, leaving the banks who financed the stock licking their wounds. As in America, the big brands will survive, though there are plenty of deals to help drain supply. Jameson’s is on semi-permanent discount in Irish supermarkets, apparently.

Irish and American whiskey share a similar business model for new entrants to the category whereby you conceive your brand, cook up some alluring backstory, buy the liquid from a contract distiller, and tell everyone your dream is to open your own distillery one day.

It all helped to inflate a big speculative bubble that has since burst. In the UK, there was a similar stampede into gin with an explosion of new brands that came and went. But with Scotch whisky, this didn’t happen because there isn’t that model of contract distilling. 

“We’ve obviously got the secondary market, and there are independent bottlers and cask investment companies, but it’s small,” says Rupert Patrick, founder & CEO of indy bottler James Eadie. “Relative to the total size of the market, it’s not even 1 per cent.”

Having worked for Diageo among other big players, he sympathises with those like Ewan Andrew tasked with trying to forecast demand in these turbulent times. “It is a massive game of chess for them,” he says. Getting predictions long or short is par for the course. “At the moment most people are probably slightly long, but maybe by 3 – 4 per cent. I don’t think by much more.”

Scotch also has various tricks up its sleeve to help manage its inventory of maturing stocks. “We’ve gone through age statements, no age statements, over-ageing, under-ageing, all sorts of things,” says Rupert. “The industry is very good at adapting to the scenario.”

Award-winning drinks columnist and author Tom Bruce-Gardyne began his career in the wine trade, managing exports for a major Sicilian producer. Now freelance for 20 years, Tom has been a weekly columnist for The Herald and his books include The Scotch Whisky Book and most recently Scotch Whisky Treasures.     According to the government’s estimates, satellite-reliant services alone underpin 18 per cent of UK GDP – which is perhaps not widely appreciated. However, one sticking point for accelerating investment in the UK’s space industry has been converting early-stage funding and innovation into commercialisation at the scale needed to ensure the UK remains competitive in the space race.

    One of the biggest changes is the government positioning itself as an “anchor customer” for the industry. A more targeted approach to funding is promised, with fewer and higher-value awards. The Strategy also promises that the UK government will “stimulate demand and use space technology through roadmaps, market insight and access pathways”.

Moving from innovative prototypes to products that are commercially viable currently requires deep pockets and a lot of patience with navigating existing red tape.     One of the regulatory objectives in the UK’s strategy is to “influence emerging international frameworks, guidelines and best practices” and the fostering of close international partnerships – for example, by working through NATO, the European Space Agency and other allies. For example, if inflation is three per cent and wage growth is four per cent in the first period, the pension will initially rise by three per cent. But if inflation then falls to two per cent while wage growth remains at four per cent in the second period, the pension will rise by five per cent to ensure it keeps pace with the cumulative eight per cent rise in wages over the full period.

    It is inconceivable that this new method can lower annual spending on pensions by £18bn by 2030. Indeed, depending on inflation and wages outcomes over the coming years, it’s possible that the changes don’t save any money at all. The public – like the bond market – should be under no illusions that this announcement will solve the UK’s economic and fiscal ills.

    Although Burnham should be commended for breaking the taboo over ending the triple lock, to raise the sums needed to fund his care plans, far more radical action on pensions would be required.     Alternatively, Policy Exchange has advocated funding social care by switching to a private insurance model, similar to the world-leading systems in Germany or Japan. In this model, workers would pay compulsory premiums from around age 40, with funding also supported by compulsory employee contributions for those below retirement age, and copayments, capped at a proportion of the total cost of the service. This would be a genuine market-based approach, a world away from the state-centred model of a National Care Service that appears to be envisioned.

    This leaves only one obvious outcome: higher taxes. As a first step, the government may seek to raise this via targeted tax increases on wealth, capital gains or high-value homes – all measures that would further damage the economy and exacerbate the flight of high-tax-paying individuals from the country. But wealth taxes have a strong track record of failure, and ultimately the sums required will require a broad-based increase in taxation – paid for by ordinary workers and businesses.

    Britain is facing an energy emergency. January bills are expected to climb by £276 for the typical UK household, the largest jump in four years, and that follows the four per cent price cap increase that arrived on 1 October. 

    Burnham’s answer so far has been a VAT cut on domestic energy bills. But all this does is move money from one pocket to another, with the taxpayer covering the difference. In the meantime, not a single bottleneck in the system is addressed. 

    The real problem lies in the friction to build. UK energy costs are high because we can’t build fast enough. The private capital and appetite to build more energy generation and infrastructure exists, but grid queues, planning delays and a lack of competition are holding us back. 

    At Fuse, we have just submitted a call to action to the UK government on how to build faster, unlock growth and bring down energy bills for good. These changes are simple, entirely within the Government’s control and don’t require subsidies or public funding. 

    First, stop making projects wait up to a decade for a grid connection. Right now, if you want to build a data centre or warehouse, even with planning permission and funding it can take up to 10 years to connect to the grid, and households pay for every month of that delay. 

    The wait is so long because the grid has to offer 24/7 access to power, so projects sit in the queue until reinforcement work is finished. Instead, we must start offering developers flexible grid connections that can be switched off when congestion is at its peak. They take on that risk in exchange for a faster connection within one to two years. More projects get on the grid, fixed grid costs get spread out more widely and household bills fall. 

    Queuing behind a monopoly

    We also need to let any qualified company build grid infrastructure instead of queuing behind a monopoly. Large grid projects should go to competitive tender by default, and network operators should pay automatic compensation to connecting customers when they miss a date. All network data, including costs, timelines and forecasts should be made public. Only with this level of accountability will things actually change. 

    When it comes to planning, we must also be better at enforcing deadlines. If the statutory period expires without a decision, the application should be approved by default. If a decision arrives late, the applicant should get their fee back. Councils and agencies would treat deadlines very differently if missing one carried a cost.

    Blocking gas turbine projects is also driving up energy costs. The more renewables we add, the more we need power that runs when the sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing. Gas fills that gap. 

    Finally, we must legalise plug-in home batteries. Plug-in solar panels became legal in the UK just a few months ago, which was the right call. But the battery, the part that lets a household store their own low cost solar power for when prices spike, is still stuck behind a safety study. Germany has years of evidence from households successfully running these systems, which we should use and build on rather than start from scratch.

    Yes, the VAT cut on domestic electricity bills will offer short term relief for households this winter. But in reality it will be spent by Spring and the Treasury will have paid for a few months of lower bills with nothing to show for it. 

    The reforms above cost nothing and ministers already hold every lever they need to bring energy costs down. If they are serious about reducing bills, make it easier to build in Britain. Don’t, and we will be having the same conversation next winter with an even bigger hole in our public finances.

    If you remember the old Alpina, before BMW took over the name, you’ll probably have a good idea of what the Bovensiepen Spider is trying to do.

    Bovensiepen is the new company built around the family behind the original Alpina, and it takes its name from founder Burkard Bovensiepen. While BMW now controls the Alpina brand itself, Bovensiepen continues to modify BMWs in much the same spirit, and the latest example, based on the BMW Z4, is the Spider.

    It gets more power from BMW’s 3.0-litre turbocharged straight-six, a revised chassis, bespoke bodywork and an interior that can be customised with plenty of leather and Alcantara. Just 99 will be built, with prices starting from €115,500, around £99,000 at current exchange rates, and customer deliveries are expected to begin in 2027.

    How much power does the Bovensiepen Spider have?

    The Spider uses BMW’s familiar 3.0-litre turbocharged straight-six, but Bovensiepen has increased output to 430bhp and almost 430lb ft of torque, up from 355bhp and 369lb ft in the standard BMW Z4 M40i.

    Power is sent through an eight-speed automatic gearbox to the rear wheels, with 0-62mph taking 4.2 seconds. That’s only three tenths quicker than the standard car, but the Spider can reach up to 183mph when fitted with the optional Performance Pack.

    The performance upgrades go beyond simply turning up the boost. Bovensiepen has fitted an unrestricted air intake with an additional ram-air channel, a larger intake silencer and a new exhaust system designed to reduce back pressure and give the straight-six a deeper sound. Cooling has also been upgraded, the suspension gets tuned dampers and longer auxiliary springs at the rear, and buyers can specify larger brakes with four-piston callipers.

    What does the Bovensiepen Performance Pack include?

    The Performance Pack adds a few more changes for buyers who want to make the most of the Spider’s extra performance. There’s an aluminium rear differential cover with larger cooling fins, an underbody V-brace to increase chassis stiffness, and the higher 183mph top speed.

    None of this turns the Z4 into a completely different car. That’s rather the point. Old Alpina was known for taking BMWs and making them faster, more luxurious and more individual without losing the character of the original car, and Bovensiepen is clearly trying to continue that approach.

    Who designed the Bovensiepen Spider?

    The Spider’s exterior has been redesigned by Frank Stephenson, the designer behind the McLaren P1 and a number of other high-profile performance cars. This isn’t his first work with Bovensiepen either, he already collaborated with the company on its 05 GT, based on the BMW M5 Touring.

    The Spider gets a new front splitter, side skirts, rear diffuser and rear spoiler, along with lightweight 20-inch forged alloy wheels. The changes are relatively subtle, which suits the Bovensiepen formula, this isn’t a BMW Z4 wearing a body kit for the sake of attracting attention. Inside, there’s more scope for personalisation too, with leather and Alcantara available in a range of combinations.

    How much does the Bovensiepen Spider cost?

    Prices start at €115,500, around £99,000, before customers start adding options, and that buys one of just 99 cars.

    That makes the Spider considerably more expensive than the BMW Z4 it’s based on. But you’re not just paying for a faster Z4, you’re paying for a limited-production car with bespoke engineering, unique styling and something the standard car has lost along the way, real exclusivity.

    The BMW Z4 has always been a slightly unusual choice in the sports car market, and Bovensiepen’s version pushes that idea further. For buyers who remember what Alpina used to represent, that’s probably the whole appeal.

    Bovensiepen Spider verdict

    The Spider doesn’t need to reinvent the Z4, and I don’t think it’s trying to. It just needs to make the old Alpina formula work for a new generation, more power, more presence, more leather, without losing what made the original cars interesting in the first place. But rational was never really the point of Alpina, old or new, and if you’re the sort of buyer who remembers what that badge used to mean, this is about as close to it as you can currently buy.

    The independent commission’s verdict on 115 charges lodged by the Premier League against Manchester City was released on Tuesday, and it details a severe case of cheating. The club deny the claims.

    But what punishment should be bestowed on the Abi Dhabi-owned team if the guilty verdicts are upheld? For that we should look back to the biggest cheating scandal in rugby.

    Back then it was Saracens setting up companies, image rights schemes and promotional payments to skirt the salary cap. They were fined over £5m for their sins and deducted enough points – in two 35-point chunks – to relegate them. They spent a year in the second-tier Championship before coming back up.

    But was that an actual punishment? A lot of that Saracens team stayed together and, while their dominance was dented, they’ve won a title since then. Fans couldn’t even mock their existence in the Championship because the season was played behind closed doors due to the Covid-19 pandemic and the reality is they were completely fine.

    Manchester City punishment will be major

    So it begs the question: what can the Premier League and the organisation’s punishers-at-large learn from the Saracens saga? Well, don’t relegate Manchester City.

    For Saracens, the relegation, while humiliating, took them away from the spotlight. Perhaps they should have been given a points deduction every year for five years; enough to stop them reaching the top four. It would have maintained their presence within the league while punishing their wrongdoing. 

    For Manchester City, that should be the main thrust of any punishment: long-term suffering without being able to market themselves as rising from the ashes.

    But beyond that there should be other learnings from rugby. Saracens weren’t placed under a transfer ban and were able to go on as normal, so long as they remained within the salary cap.

    The Premier League should get creative with Manchester City: keep any money raised from player sales for non-league clubs in trouble; implement a complete transfer ban on players; only allow them to sign English players on loan; and ensure the punishment is visible to all who care – mainly fans.

    Level playing field

    Sport is never really a level playing field and I am not sure anyone believes it ever has been. And with that, punishments should ensure that something is given back in return for all that has been taken.

    What the Premier League commission’s findings show is that brazen attempts to skirt – albeit arbitrary – footballing rules will be found out, eventually at least.

    How different organisations across sport react to that varies. The NBA’s LA Clippers were slapped with a $30m fine and their owner Steve Ballmer was banned from a year’s worth of games for paying Kawhi Leonard extra via back-door schemes.

    Yet Saracens were allowed to quietly go about their business and return without a major hit, comparatively speaking at least.

    So Manchester City is an interesting test case. And it is something the Premier League can use to deter others while ensuring that fans feel like their outrage has been heard.

    Once viewed as stuffy and outdated, the tie is staging a comeback. adam bloodworth explores how the corporate staple is being reclaimed by musicians and London’s underground club scene

    For generations of men, the tie was something you wore without thinking. Slipping one on was simply part of your morning routine, as mundane as shaving or splashing on some cologne. But then the shadow of Big Tech loomed over the corporate world, with its hoodies and its t-shirts and its trainers.

    The tie became a symbol of the old world order, something stuffy and irrelevant. Who has time to tie a double Windsor when you should be moving fast and breaking things? And then came the pandemic, with its work-from-home ethos that allowed people to Zoom into meetings wearing their pyjamas. Nobody is getting suited-up to sit at a desk in their spare room.

    I noticed this at 4am in London’s Docklands, where thousands of people were dancing in the former Guinness factory. The brutalist building, now home to the Cause, one of the capital’s hippest clubs, throbbed with bass. On the dance floor, people tend to wear next to nothing, largely to cope with the heat but also to feel sexy and to attract the wandering eye. Leather shorts, harnesses and sunglasses are par for the course. But more surprising were the number of ties, their Macclesfield, polka dot or tartan designs flashing in the strobe lights.

    The tie might be back.

    The tie, I realised, has become ironically cool.

    “Ties have usually been associated with corporate culture, so when a queer person takes a garment with that type of connotation and applies it to club culture, there’s an element of reclaiming something ordinary and making it theatrical,” says Jordan Wake, a style writer for Vogue. “When I’ve spotted someone wearing a tie on a dancefloor, it’s usually styled with something like a skirt and a pair of heels,” says Wake. “It makes sense that something as simple as a tie would work its way into these spaces.”

    Indeed, a broader shift is emerging, rocketing the humble accessory to new, unfathomable levels of clout. It’s no longer just office workers and club kids; silken, multicoloured neckties are everywhere. The autumn/winter 2026 runways were awash with them. In Milan, Ralph Lauren models wore skinny silk ties; Prada and Dolce & Gabbana dropped tonally complex versions and, in Paris, Louis Vuitton experimented with academic-chic, layering ties beneath knitwear, while Junya Watanabe sent models out wearing multiple ties at once; in London, Paul Smith debuted a range of ties with floral detailing.

    For Spencer Riley, design director at Charles Tyrwhitt, the rise of neckwear is a pushback against the overly casual, work-from-home attire popularised in the early 2020s. People miss dressing up and feeling great. “I remember thinking ties were a thing of the past,” says Riley. “But by 2024, it became clear that ‘status’ was going to become a bigger influence on how men wanted to dress, and the tie started to come back.”

    In innovation terms, unsurprisingly, London is leading the charge. This summer, Harry Styles was never far away from a tie during his Wembley Stadium tour (one, a floral number by the British label JW, celebrated homegrown tailoring); Elle Fanning was deemed a ‘girlboss’ for wearing one at a photocall in the capital last year for new musical drama A Complete Unknown; and 1960s icon Twiggy proved the androgynous look isn’t only for the young, pairing a black smoking jacket with a black tie during Burberry’s autumn/winter 2025 showcase.

    “People are seeing ties on celebrities, influencers and sportsmen and recognising that they can instantly elevate an outfit,” says Riley. “It’s become a fashion trend as much as a formal accessory. For younger men especially, the tie can feel like a relatively simple way of making a statement.”

    It’s also a financial statement: fashion marketplace Depop reported a 31 per cent increase in tie sales in 2025, while the global tie market’s valuation has grown from $3.7bn to $4bn, according to the oddly specific Grand View Research Neckwear Market Report.

    Bold, block colours, and wide 1980s-coded ties are out, with designers preferring subtler designs that nonetheless display character. They might be swaying down catwalks, but it’d be wrong to assume the ironic reclaiming of the tie is tied to sartorial brashness. “Rather than the bright colours and obvious patterns we saw in the past, there’s been a move towards more tonal, textural and complementary styles,” says Riley, pointing to the popularity of Charles Tyrwhitt’s 2026 Grenadine range, which features light, open weave, hand-made pieces. “Grenadine is a great example because it adds interest without overpowering the rest of the outfit.”

    For Gabriella Brick, head of design at Moss Bros, experimentation is key. “The way in which we are styling ties demonstrates how much diversity you can create, whether that’s pairing them with an Italian contrast collar shirt, a button-down Oxford, or even a denim shirt. Ties are no longer just for formal looks.”

    None of this is new, really. The relatively straightforward, contemporary tie is the debauched younger sibling of the elaborate cravat, once de rigueur in high society. These Regency-era staples were a faff to tie, although for the era’s dandies, it was an essential signal of one’s status; from the late 1700s the mess of colour around your neck was a definitive marker of wealth. Workers wore versions cut from cheaper cotton (aristos would baulk at a necktie not made from starched white linen, or some fabulous imported muslin, another signal of their financial status).

    More than just the material, the colour – starched white – was a symbol of status, showing the owner had access to a washing machine. On the contrary, workers often chose their ties in darker colours to hide the stains.

    The tie as we know it rocketed to popularity in the 1880s, when students at Oxford University’s Exeter College ripped the ribbons from their hats to tie them around their necks, creating the timeless necktie design now synonymous with education and university graduation. In the 1920s, tailors figured out how to cut the material en masse, allowing the first mass-production ties made from cotton, wool and tweed.

    Hay Fever review and star rating: ★★★★

    Of course, darling: Richard E Grant simply must play David Bliss, the blinkered, posho patriarch at the centre of Noel Coward’s drawing room comedy, Hay Fever. This is how I imagine the casting conversations went, anyway. Shockingly, E Grant – everyone’s favourite aristo-portrayer – has until now never starred in a Coward play, so here is his moment. He is delicious as the delusional novelist in Emily Burns’ Hay Fever, the latest proof that Coward is still more than capable of summing up our 21st century idiosyncrasies fifty odd years after his death. 

    You think these people are too flatly ridiculous to exist, and then you remember you know countless people like them. We’re in the Bliss household in the village of Cookham, Berkshire, where retired actress Judith Bliss is wafting around declaring that she is to make a return to the stage, although you suspect she says the same thing every day. Christine Baranski brings both heft and hilarity to the ludicrously delusional matriarch; her barbs drop heavily, but always dressed to the nines, she has a weightlessness, too (Judith is a fusing of two actual women Coward knew, one a New York socialite and one from London; the former loved the portrayal but the latter was deeply offended). 

    Richard E Grant in Hay Fever

    Essentially nothing much is going on, except that all four of the Bliss family, including son Simon and daughter Sorel, have invited guests to stay for the weekend. The incoming troupe, including Nancy Carroll’s London society type Myra and Ash Hunter’s amateur boxer Sandy Tyrell, are confronted by the family’s constant squabbling and petulant behaviour until they’re driven up the wall, and unite to draw up a drastic escape plan.

    Coward’s central depiction of an exasperated couple still stings with contemporaneity, and the best lines derive from Judith and David’s explosive tiffs. As Myra states of the couple, “you’re artificial to the point of lunacy.” 

    He’s magnetic to watch self-destruct

    Richard E Grant is obviously perfect for the feverishly privileged, short tempered David, who, like so many poshos, is magnetic to watch self-destruct. I could watch the actor play angry, bellowing, gesticulating toffs for literal years, even if Saltburn, Withnail & I and the countless other roles have tended to typecast him. Baranski grips equally, flipping in milliseconds between sensual and ballistic, drawing on her Mamma Mia film performance to produce a decent English accent (Maggie Smith premiered the part at the Old Vic in 1964, when the play become the National Theatre’s first production of a play by a living author).

    Burns’ conventional but sparkling production proves Coward is still an absolute king of farce.

    Hay Fever plays at the Wyndham’s Theatre until 12 December

    On 25 September 1978, John Peel played Teenage Kicks, the debut single from The Undertones, on his Radio 1 evening show. Two minutes and 28 seconds later, in a brazen breach of BBC protocol, he played the same song for a second time, telling listeners “it doesn’t get much better than this”. 

    I recently had an ‘instant replay’ moment of my own, driving on the Route Napoleon in the French Alps. This glorious road was used for the car chase in Goldeneye, with James Bond (Pierce Brosnan) manhandling an Aston Martin DB5, pursued by Xenia Onatopp in a Ferrari F355. The most spectacular section weaves through a series of steeply stacked hairpins, then clings to the cliff edge, cutting through natural arches in the jagged limestone rock.

    It’s a stretch of tarmac so dramatic, challenging and exhilarating that, when I reached a roundabout, I couldn’t resist turning around and immediately doing it all again. Because it really doesn’t get much better than this, whether you’re driving a blue-blooded supercar or a battery-electric Kia. 

    A new kind of electric performance 

    If that sounds a bit hyperbolic, take note that the EV4 GT is not a common-or-garden Kia. Indeed, with dual motors, all-wheel drive, bigger brakes, adaptive dampers, electronic torque vectoring, Kia’s Virtual Gear Shift system and Pirelli P Zero tyres, it has aspirations to be a proper hot hatchback.

    In recent years, ever-tighter legislation and emissions targets have made such cars into an endangered species. Many have been killed off with no successor in sight, among them the Ford Focus ST, Hyundai i30 N, Renault Megane RS and Honda Civic Type R. For somebody who got his teenage kicks driving hot hatches, this decline has been sad to see. 

    Thankfully, a new breed of electric hot hatches has begun to emerge. If you want something supermini-sized, you can consider the Alpine A290 GTS, Vauxhall Corsa GSE or Peugeot 208 GTI. And at the top end of the market, there is the impressive Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, which resembles a hatchback but has the stature of an SUV.

    Until now, though, no credible EV contender has targeted the hot hatch heartland inhabited by the Volkswagen Golf GTI. That’s where the Kia comes in. 

    Kia EV GT prices and spec

    At £49,345, the EV4 GT is pricier than an entry-level Golf GTI (£41,860) or indeed a Golf R (£46,930). However, being powered by batteries should make for much lower running costs than either – provided you have an EV charger installed at home. 

    Kia also offers its famous seven year, 100,000-mile warranty, plus a long list of standard equipment. The fully loaded GT spec includes intelligent LED headlights, heated and ventilated front seats, 360-degree parking cameras, ambient interior lighting, an electric tailgate and an eight-speaker Harman Kardon sound system. The only option of note is ‘premium’ paint, such as the Blue Flame colour seen here (£650).

    You can tell the GT apart from a regular EV4 by its beefier bumpers, gloss-black trim and neon green brake calipers, which are tucked inside 20-inch alloy wheels. Inside, there’s more neon green on the seatbelts and dashboard, along with alloy pedals and bucket seats trimmed in faux leather and suede. 

    You want numbers? Zero to 62mph takes 5.6 seconds, top speed is 105mph and kerb weight is 2,060kg. The EV-specific stats are 81.4kWh (size of the lithium-ion battery), 128kW (maximum charging speed) 3.4 miles per kWh (energy consumption) and 313 miles (driving range in the official WLTP test).

    The Kia GT story so far

    Kia’s GT badge has been around since the bizarrely punctuated Pro_cee’d GT of 2013. However, apart from the flagship 585hp EV6 GT, the vehicles it was affixed to have been ‘warm’ rather than explicitly hot. They were all overshadowed by sister brand Hyundai’s more extroverted and exciting ‘N’ cars, too.

    This is the first GT model developed from scratch by Manfred Harrer, Kia’s head of R&D since 2025, whose CV includes 14 years at Porsche. It slots into the range between the also-new EV3 GT crossover and EV5 GT SUV, but is the most overtly sporting of the trio. It’s expected to be the best-seller, too – although the EV4 GT exists more to boost Kia’s image than its bottom line. 

    All of which brings us to a hotel car park somewhere north of Nice. The Mediterranean sun is shining, the EV4 GT is brimmed with fresh electrons and the route snakes across its sat-nav screen like tangled strands of spaghetti. Yep, we’ve all had worse days at work.

    Fun for all the family

    Kia’s futuristic ‘Opposites United’ design language works well on an SUV, but looks slab-sided and not particularly sporting here. Still, many will appreciate the GT’s ability to speak softly and carry a 292 horsepower stick. 

    The advantage of that boxy body is plenty of passenger space, helped by the EV4’s ‘skateboard’ platform and flat floor. There’s room for three adults in the back, plus useful stowage in the deep door bins, centre armrest and seat-back pockets. There is no ‘frunk’ and the extra electric motor for the rear axle does rob some boot capacity, however. A total of 377 litres is 58 litres smaller than a standard EV4. 

    Finding a good driving position is easy and the electric seats hug you in the right places. Kia’s in-car tech is also straightforward to use, with a 12.3-inch central touchscreen that syncs wirelessly with your smartphone via Apple CarPlay or Android Auto. The GT even has a data logger to measure your driving performance in real time. 

    Inside the Kia EV4 GT

    Despite the on-board telemetry and the presence of a new GT mode, Kia insists the hottest EV4 is ‘neither an out-and-out performance car, nor a track-day weapon’. The emphasis here, we’re told, is on ‘everyday usable power’ and a ‘familiar, comfortable character’. 

    Accordingly, in the bustle of Nice’s morning rush-hour, the EV4 delivers relaxed, unobtrusive progress. It’s as easy to drive as any electric Kia, with light steering, a hushed soundtrack and decent all-round visibility. There’s also a full complement of electronic driver aids, such as blind-spot monitors and rear cross-traffic assist (to warn of approaching cars when you reverse out of a parking space).

    In Normal mode, the Kia also has a commendably pliant ride, helped by a camera-based system that scans the road surface, preparing the dampers for what lies ahead. And today, as the Cote d’Azur soars majestically upwards into the Alpes-Maritimes, that means some of Europe’s very best driving roads. Route Napoleon, here we come.

    A hotter way to go green

    Push the neon green GT mode toggle on its steering wheel and the EV4 instantly feels energised. Its straight-line performance isn’t scorching by hot hatch standards – the latest Golf R is a second quicker to 62mph –  but the combination of all-wheel drive and an ever-ready 345lb ft of electric torque will slingshot you out of corners. On rural French D-roads, it gets you past dawdling motorhomes quickly and safely, too.

    Kia has set up the GT to be primarily front-driven, in search of traditional hot hatchback handling balance (and more predictable behaviour at the limit, no doubt). Be abrupt with your right foot and all that can overwhelm the front wheels, leading to a scrabble for traction, but such instances are rare. For the most part, the EV4 feels calm and controlled, with limited body-roll and resolute grip from its EV-optimised rubber. 

    Coming back to our Golf R comparison, the Kia has a similar ability to cover ground quickly, making light work of difficult roads. Its steering isn’t the last word in feedback and the regenerative brakes sometimes feel inconsistent. But it’s fun in a grown-up kind of way.

    Like a video game made real

    If you want something more involving/intriguing/immature (delete as appropriate), you can play with the Virtual Gear Shift. Previously seen in the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, this simulates a six-speed manual transmission, accompanied by the snarl of a powerful petrol engine.

    At first, the effect feels rather like playing a video game, but you soon forget the artifice and just enjoy the experience. Leave the VGS in automatic mode and it gives a convincing impression of a twin-clutch auto ’box. Alternatively, you can take control via paddles behind the steering wheel, which are otherwise used to adjust the level of brake energy recovery. The ‘redline’ is at 6,000rpm and you run out of revs at 7,100rpm, causing a lurch as the ‘engine’ bounces off its imaginary limiter. You can’t stall, but well-timed shifts are rewarded with swift, smooth progress.

    As for the soundtrack, a member of Kia’s PR team likened it to the five-cylinder engine in an Audi RS3 and I can’t think of a better comparison. It’s quite different to the hot Hyundai, which has eight virtual gears and sounds more like a turbocharged four.  

    Verdict: Kia EV4 GT

    To paraphrase Mark Twain, reports of the hot hatchback’s death have been greatly exaggerated. Indeed, cars like the EV4 GT offer hope that an electric future doesn’t need to be dull. And if a part of their appeal lies in imitating a petrol car, so be it. If you don’t like the Virtual Gear Shift and five-cylinder fireworks, you can switch them off. 

    Ultimately, the EV4 GT isn’t as entertaining as the benchmark Golf GTI, but it’s a quick and accomplished car that delivers on Kia’s goals to be comfortable and usable. If you’re in the market for a family EV and want more than just fuss-free transport and a long warranty, it’s well worth a look. 

    Who knows, you might even find yourself tackling a great road just for the fun of it. If you’re in the area, may I recommend the Route Napoleon? Just allow yourself enough time to drive it twice.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing. Vinted makes its money almost entirely from the buyer’s side of the transaction: a fixed fee of roughly $0.70 plus a variable fee of about 5 percent of the item’s price, charged in the buyer’s local currency (figures as of late 2025) — according to Vinted’s own Buyer Protection fee page. An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.
